sections.overview: The Eurasian tree sparrow is a small, sociable sparrow of farmland edges. In Britain it has suffered a severe long-term decline, and it is a Red-listed species there despite a recent small recovery from a very low level.
sections.identification: Slightly smaller than a house sparrow, an adult weighs about 21 g and has a wing length near 70 mm. It has a chestnut crown and nape, white cheeks with a black spot, a small black bib and a streaky brown back. Males and females look alike, and juveniles resemble faded adults.
sections.habitat: In Britain and Ireland it lives mainly in eastern and lowland areas and is most frequent on arable farmland in the breeding season. In winter it gathers in flocks on stubble fields and sometimes visits garden feeders in rural villages.
sections.diet: It eats seeds of grasses and weeds and cultivated grain such as barley and wheat, and catches small insects to feed its young. Chicks fed more seed and fewer invertebrates fledged less successfully in one study.
sections.behavior: It is social, breeding in small loose colonies, and shyer and less boisterous than the house sparrow, often holding its tail up. Outside the breeding season it can travel considerable distances, and some breeding areas are vacated entirely in winter.
sections.reproduction: It nests in holes and crevices in buildings, banks, cliffs and nest boxes. The breeding season runs from April to August, with one or two broods of typically five or six eggs. Both sexes incubate for 12–13 days, and the chicks fledge after about 15–17.5 days. Breeding typically starts at one year.
sections.ecology: Breeding success is linked to the invertebrate prey fed to the chicks, and in winter birds gather where seed food is available. A typical adult lives about two years, and the oldest ringed bird reached nearly eleven.
sections.conservation: The IUCN Red List classes it as Least Concern, but in the UK it is Red-listed. UK numbers fell by an estimated 93% between 1970 and 2008; the breeding population was 245,000 territories in 2016, up 18% since 1995 but far below 1970s levels. In Europe it has declined since 1980.
